description: Every lab and route boopis can set up: sign-ins, API keys, models on this computer and endpoints of your own (ADR-0039). One reviewed file, read by the host (apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/providers, with include_str!), the UI (apps/desktop/ui/src/data/providers.ts) and the plugin (a copy made by scripts/sync-shared-data.sh); the readers are tested against `examples`. To add a lab: one entry here, and an example. An entry is a lab (or a host, or a runtime on this computer) with the ways to connect to it; the array is the display order, `rank` is the research ranking (equal for ties, ADR-0039), and `shown` says whether setup and Settings list it by default or under More providers (search always finds every entry that is not hidden). A way is one route: `kind` signin, key, local or custom; `engine` is the provider slug exactly as the engine spells it (`model.provider` and the `<slug>/<model>` of a ladder tier), cited in `engine_source`; for a custom endpoint or a runtime written as one, `slug` is the name of the `providers.<slug>` entry boopis writes. Key variables are the names the engine reads, in its order; `key.wire_var` is the one boopis binds to the keychain secret `secret://provider.<engine or slug>/api_key`. Labels, hints and notes are boopis's own words and never name the engine (ADR-0031); notes marked `terms` are the owner's to approve. Setup and Settings are drawn from this file, never from a list in code. Routes that are not offered yet are in `not_offered`, with who they wait for.

engine.about: The engine release every `engine_source` and slug was read from. A new engine release is a reason to re-read them, not to change them blind.

heavy_switches.label: Climb to Fable
heavy_switches.reason: Fable is token-heavy: Ramp's benchmark measured $3.79 a task against Opus's $1.53, and on a Claude Pro plan it bills usage credits from the first request. So boopis never adds it by itself. Off: governed work stays on Opus, and a failed gate retries there. On: Fable is the top tier, and a failed gate climbs to it.
heavy_switches.not_applicable: The saved ladder is not a Claude one, so there is no Fable choice to make. Change models sets that up.

heavy_switches.label: Use Grok
heavy_switches.reason: Grok 4.7 is token-heavy: Ramp's benchmark measured it at $4.32 a task, with the most tool calls of any model (161 a task). So boopis never adds it by itself. Off: boopis does not run governed work on it. On: Grok is the top tier of the ladder.
heavy_switches.not_applicable: There is no xAI key, or the saved ladder is not an xAI one, so there is no Grok choice to make. Change models sets that up.
heavy_switches.none_listed: Your xAI key lists no Grok 4.7 or later, so there is nothing to turn on.

heavy_switches.label: Use Gemini 4 Carbon
heavy_switches.reason: Gemini 4 Carbon is the costliest frontier model in Ramp's benchmark: $5.19 a task against Neon's $4.38 and Hydrogen's $3.24, and it solved 72.6% where Neon solved 76.2%. So boopis never adds it by itself. Off: governed work stays on Hydrogen and Neon. On: Carbon is the top tier of the ladder.
heavy_switches.not_applicable: There is no Google key, or the saved ladder is not a Gemini one, so there is no Carbon choice to make. Change models sets that up.
heavy_switches.none_listed: Your Google key lists no Gemini 4 Carbon or later, so there is nothing to turn on.

never_frontier.about: Custom endpoints and models on this computer are never frontier (fail closed, ADR-0037 and ADR-0039), so they can never run governed mode, whatever their model is called. A model is never frontier when its provider is in `engines` or starts with one of `slug_prefixes`; every other provider is judged by the model's name as before. The three readers of frontier-models.json apply this first.

endpoint.about: The form for adding an endpoint of your own (form kind `endpoint`, docs/FORMS.md) and what `provider_test_endpoint` and `provider_add_endpoint` accept. The form is the host's own: its secret field goes to the command, never to the keychain by the card and never into text on the page.

examples.why: plain http is allowed only on this computer

slug.rule: custom- + the name in lower case, runs of anything but letters and digits as one dash, dashes trimmed, cut to 40 characters; when taken, -2, -3 and so on

test.about: One GET per path, the first that answers wins. The key, when there is one, is sent as the API mode says (a bearer token for the OpenAI modes, x-api-key for Anthropic) and only to the address typed.

not_offered.route: Google AI Pro or Ultra sign-in
not_offered.why: Google offers no sanctioned way for another app to use a consumer Google AI subscription. Not offered.
Z.ai limits the plan to listed tools and boopis is not on the list. No coding-plan endpoint is added.
Kimi limits the membership to the tools it lists and boopis is not one. No coding-plan endpoint is added, and a key that starts with sk-kimi- is turned down.
The plan's terms for other apps were not found.
The engine has one, but only a key is offered.
Nous Portal is the engine maker's own model service, not a consumer lab (owner, 21 November 2026): a key only, under More providers. The free tier (ADR-0027) is separate and unchanged.
Cloud routes (Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry) are a later wave: one Cloud group, with the cloud's own credentials chain and nothing stored by boopis. A hand-written configuration still works.

spikes.question: Which provider slug does a direct OpenAI API key use in the engine: `openai` or `openai-api`?
spikes.result: `openai-api`. It is a registry row, not a plugin: id `openai-api`, key variable OPENAI_API_KEY, base URL variable OPENAI_BASE_URL, default https://api.openai.com/v1, wire `codex_responses`. The slug `openai` is wrong for the key: the engine's provider table lists it as a legacy alias of `openrouter`, so a model.provider of `openai` would send the key to OpenRouter's route. The ChatGPT subscription is a different slug, `openai-codex`. The `openai` spelling in boopis's own data (frontier examples, the names table) is harmless for the frontier match, which is by model name, but the names table's dispatch entry should say `openai-api`.
evidence: hermes_cli/providers.py HERMES_OVERLAYS: "openai-api" with transport codex_responses, base_url_override https://api.openai.com/v1, base_url_env_var OPENAI_BASE_URL

hermes_cli/providers.py _ALIAS_GROUPS: "openrouter": ("openai",), so normalize_provider("openai") is "openrouter"; resolve_provider_full tries a user-written providers.openai first, which is why that one is not hijacked

hermes_cli/models_catalog_static.py: CANONICAL_PROVIDERS has ("openai-api", "OpenAI API", ...) and _PROVIDER_MODELS["openai-api"] is the curated list; PROVIDER_GROUPS["openai"] is the picker group ["openai-codex", "openai-api"]
hermes_cli/models_validate.py: for openai and openai-api on an official OpenAI host the live listing is final, so a model the key cannot list is rejected rather than soft-accepted
hermes_cli/auth.py _openrouter_auto_detected: OPENAI_API_KEY counts as an OpenRouter key only when it looks like one; a real OpenAI key falls through to the `openai-api` row
hermes_cli/main_provider_setup.py _GENERIC_API_KEY_PROVIDERS lists `openai-api` among the plain key providers
spikes.decision: Setup writes model.provider `openai-api`, binds OPENAI_API_KEY to secret://provider.openai-api/api_key, and the ladder tier reads openai-api/<model>.
